subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Japanese vs. Chinese Green Tea
description: One-minute skill: Japanese vs. Chinese Green Tea.

hook.text: Japanese and Chinese green teas taste nothing alike—even though they're the same type of tea.

buildup.text: Chinese green tea is pan-fired in a wok to stop oxidation. This gives it a toasty, nutty character.

discovery.text: Japanese green tea is steamed instead. Steaming preserves a vivid green color and a grassy, marine flavor.

twist.text: The difference is just seconds of heat applied differently. The same leaf, two techniques, two worlds of flavor.

climax.text: Chinese Longjing and Japanese Sencha are both green teas, but they'd fool anyone into thinking otherwise.

punchline.text: Pan-fired vs. steamed. One choice, two entirely different teas.

quiz.question: How do Japanese and Chinese green teas differ in processing?
options: Japan steams; China pan-fires the leaves

details.summary: Japanese and Chinese green teas taste fundamentally different because of how oxidation is halted. Japanese teas are steamed, creating bright green color and umami-rich marine flavors. Chinese teas are pan-fired in a wok, producing a more toasty, nutty, and mellow character.
details.whyItMatters: The steam-versus-fire distinction is the single biggest flavor divide in green tea. It explains why Japanese and Chinese greens taste like different drinks.
takeaways: Japanese green teas are steamed for a vegetal, umami flavor
Chinese green teas are pan-fired for toasty, mellow notes
The kill-green method is the primary flavor difference

faq.question: Which country produces more green tea overall?
faq.answer: China produces roughly 80 percent of the world's green tea by volume. Japan produces far less but consumes most domestically. Chinese green tea dominates global exports, while Japanese teas like matcha and sencha occupy the premium segment.

faq.question: Why does Japanese green tea taste so different?
faq.answer: Steaming preserves chlorophyll and amino acids, especially L-theanine, which gives Japanese teas their characteristic umami and bright green color. Shade-growing before harvest further boosts these compounds. Pan-firing Chinese greens develop different flavors through dry heat.
